result.summary: 11 requirements (6 functional, 5 non-functional); 20 ambiguities resolved as assumptions, 0 unresolved.

outputs.goal: Provide a locally runnable HTTP service that creates shareable short links for validated HTTP/HTTPS URLs and redirects visitors to their destinations. Provide public link metadata, token-authorized deletion, expiry handling, and an operations health endpoint.

functional.text: Create a link with POST /api/links using a JSON body with required `url` and optional `alias` and `expiresAt` fields. Return HTTP 201 with the code, relative `shortPath`, and a management token that is returned only in the creation response. Generated codes are 8 characters from `[A-Za-z0-9_-]`, case-sensitive. Custom aliases are 3–32 characters from `[A-Za-z0-9_-]`, case-sensitive; reject reserved service paths and invalid aliases with HTTP 400. Reject a custom alias already assigned to an active or tombstoned link with HTTP 409.
Accept an optional future expiry timestamp in UTC. At or after that instant, do not redirect the link; return HTTP 410 Gone. Expiry does not delete the link or prevent public metadata retrieval.

GET /{code} redirects an active, unexpired link to its original URL using HTTP 302 Found and a Location header. Do not cache redirect responses. Return HTTP 410 Gone for expired links and HTTP 404 Not Found for unknown or deleted codes.

GET /api/links/{code} returns public metadata for a non-deleted link: original URL, creation timestamp, and expiry timestamp (null when no expiry is set). Return HTTP 404 Not Found for unknown or deleted codes. Expired links remain available through this endpoint.

DELETE /api/links/{code} requires the link's management token in the X-Management-Token header. Return HTTP 204 No Content on successful deletion; return HTTP 401 for a missing token, HTTP 403 for an invalid token, and HTTP 404 for an unknown or already-deleted code. Deletion retains a tombstone reserving the code and erases the destination URL; neither generated codes nor custom aliases are reused. Store only a hash of the management token, never the plaintext token.
GET /health provides an operations health check, returning HTTP 200 when the service and its persistence store are available and HTTP 503 otherwise.

non_functional.text: An automated indicative performance check must measure 1,000 redirect requests after a warm-up, from a single client on the local machine, and assert p99 latency below 50 ms in-process. This check is not a production SLO.

Accept only syntactically valid HTTP or HTTPS URLs up to 2,048 characters. At creation, reject localhost and any host that is itself or resolves to a loopback, private, link-local, unique-local, or multicast IPv4 or IPv6 address. Check DNS-resolved addresses once at creation; DNS changes after creation are an accepted limitation. The service must not fetch destination URLs.

Protect link creation with an in-memory Bucket4j rate limit of 20 create requests per minute per client IP. Return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header when limited. A service restart resets the limit state.
Run locally with one command and no external infrastructure. Persist links and tombstones across restarts using file-based H2 under ./data, with Flyway-managed schema migrations.

Provide automated tests covering each functional flow and important failure paths, including URL and alias validation, expiry, deletion authorization, rate limiting, persistence across restart, and redirect latency.

ambiguities.question: What characters, length limits, and case-sensitivity rules apply to custom aliases?
ambiguities.resolution: Custom aliases are 3-32 characters from [A-Za-z0-9_-], case-sensitive (consistent with generated codes). Reserved words are rejected: api, health, links (and any path the service itself uses).
ambiguities.rationale: Decided by a human: Apply the provided alias constraints and reserve every service route so aliases cannot shadow endpoints.

ambiguities.question: What rate limit applies to link creation, over what interval, and how are clients identified (for example, by IP address)?
ambiguities.resolution: 20 link creations per minute per client IP address. Exceeding it returns 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header. Limits are held in memory (Bucket4j); a restart resets them. Interpret this as a bucket with capacity 20 refilled at 20 per minute; count requests to the create endpoint, including rejected attempts.
ambiguities.rationale: Decided by a human: The threshold, interval, response, storage, and library are binding; a 20-token bucket and counting all create requests are conventional abuse-resistant interpretations.

ambiguities.question: Who is allowed to fetch metadata or delete a link, and is authentication or authorization required?
ambiguities.resolution: Metadata (GET) is public. Creating a link returns a one-time management token; DELETE requires that token (e.g. an X-Management-Token header), so only the creator can delete. No user accounts in v1. Store only a hash of the token, never the token itself.
ambiguities.rationale: Decided by a human: Implement public metadata and token-based deletion without user accounts, and persist no plaintext management token.

ambiguities.question: Must links survive service restarts, and where should local link data be stored?
ambiguities.resolution: Yes, links must survive restarts. Use file-based H2 under ./data with Flyway-managed schema migrations.
ambiguities.rationale: Decided by a human: Use the specified local H2 file store and Flyway migrations as the persistence design.

ambiguities.question: Precisely which destinations count as malicious or internal, and should validation cover DNS-resolved addresses, IPv4, IPv6, and address changes over time?
ambiguities.resolution: Accept only http/https URLs up to 2048 characters. Reject localhost and any host that is, or resolves to, a loopback, private, link-local, unique-local or multicast address (IPv4 and IPv6), checked once at creation. Re-pointing DNS after creation is an accepted, documented limitation: the service never fetches the URL.
ambiguities.rationale: Decided by a human: Enforce the specified schemes, length, address classes, one-time DNS check, and no-fetch limitation.

ambiguities.question: What traffic volume, concurrency, measurement window, and runtime conditions define the p99 latency target?
ambiguities.resolution: Measured in-process by an automated test: 1,000 redirect requests after a warm-up, single client, local machine, asserting p99 < 50 ms. Documented as an indicative check, not a production SLO.
ambiguities.rationale: Decided by a human: Use the specified test scope and treat the result as indicative rather than a production guarantee.

ambiguities.question: After deletion, may a short code or custom alias be reused for a new link?
ambiguities.resolution: No. Codes and custom aliases are never reused. Deleting a link keeps a tombstone record that reserves the code and erases the destination URL; a deleted code returns 404 like an unknown one, and creating a link with a deleted alias returns 409 Conflict.
ambiguities.rationale: Decided by a human: Retain tombstones, erase the destination, and permanently reserve deleted codes and aliases.

ambiguities.question: What short-code length and alphabet should generated codes use?
ambiguities.resolution: Use 8-character generated codes from [A-Za-z0-9_-], case-sensitive. Regenerate a code if it collides with an active code, tombstone, or service route.
ambiguities.rationale: The requirement leaves generated-code format open; an 8-character URL-safe code provides a practical namespace, and retrying collisions is a standard low-risk implementation.

ambiguities.question: What redirect status code should the service return (301 vs 302)?
ambiguities.resolution: Return 302 Found and include Cache-Control: no-store.
ambiguities.rationale: A temporary redirect is safer because links can expire or be deleted; preventing caching helps those changes take effect for subsequent visits.

ambiguities.question: What should happen when a custom alias is already taken?
ambiguities.resolution: Return HTTP 409 Conflict for an alias assigned to either an active link or a tombstone.
ambiguities.rationale: A conflict response is the conventional way to report a unique-resource naming collision and is consistent with the human decision that deleted aliases remain reserved.

ambiguities.question: What HTTP paths, payload fields, and successful response bodies should the v1 API use?
ambiguities.resolution: Use POST /api/links with JSON fields `url`, optional `alias`, and optional `expiresAt`; return 201 with `code`, `shortPath`, and `managementToken`. Use GET /{code} for redirects, GET /api/links/{code} for metadata, DELETE /api/links/{code} for deletion, and GET /health for health. Metadata fields are `originalUrl`, `createdAt`, and `expiresAt`.
ambiguities.rationale: The requirement names the operations but not their contract; these conventional REST routes and explicit fields make the v1 API testable without adding capabilities.

ambiguities.question: What format should expiry use, and how should an expiry at or before creation time be handled?
ambiguities.resolution: Use an ISO-8601 UTC instant in the `expiresAt` field, normalize returned timestamps to UTC, and reject an expiry at or before creation time with HTTP 400.
ambiguities.rationale: An explicit UTC instant is an unambiguous conventional timestamp format; rejecting a non-future expiry avoids creating a link that is already expired.

ambiguities.question: What response behavior should apply to unknown, deleted, expired, malformed, and unauthorized requests?
ambiguities.resolution: Return HTTP 400 for malformed or invalid create input, 409 for a taken alias, 429 with Retry-After when rate-limited, 302 for an active redirect, 410 for an expired redirect, and 404 for an unknown or deleted code. Metadata for an expired non-deleted link returns 200; metadata for an unknown or deleted code returns 404. On deletion, return 401 for a missing token, 403 for an invalid token, 204 on success, and 404 for an unknown or deleted code.
ambiguities.rationale: The requirement does not define error statuses; these standard distinctions make failures observable, while 410 distinguishes expiry from an unknown or deleted link.

ambiguities.question: Should the create response contain an absolute short URL, and how is its public origin determined?
ambiguities.resolution: Return the relative `shortPath` and code, not an absolute URL; clients combine the path with the service origin they already use.
ambiguities.rationale: The requirement does not define a canonical public origin; returning a relative path avoids trusting request Host or proxy headers and needs no deployment configuration.

ambiguities.question: How should the management token be generated, exposed, and validated?
ambiguities.resolution: Generate a cryptographically random 256-bit token, encode it as unpadded base64url, return it only in the creation response, and store a SHA-256 hash. Accept it in X-Management-Token and keep it valid until successful deletion; do not persist or log the plaintext token.
ambiguities.rationale: High-entropy random bearer tokens and one-time display with hash-only storage are conventional safeguards for a token that authorizes deletion.

ambiguities.question: What should happen if DNS resolution fails or returns both allowed and prohibited addresses during URL validation?
ambiguities.resolution: Fail closed: reject the URL if resolution fails, times out, yields no usable address, or any returned address is prohibited.
ambiguities.rationale: Failing closed is the low-risk interpretation of the requirement to reject hosts that resolve to prohibited destinations.

ambiguities.question: How should the service identify a client IP when requests may include forwarding headers?
ambiguities.resolution: Use the network peer address by default and do not trust forwarding headers unless a trusted-proxy configuration is explicitly provided.
ambiguities.rationale: The service has no specified proxy deployment; using the peer address avoids spoofable client-supplied headers and is a safe local default.

ambiguities.question: What does the health endpoint check?
ambiguities.resolution: Return HTTP 200 with an UP status when the service and H2 store are available; return HTTP 503 otherwise.
ambiguities.rationale: Checking both the application and the persistence store is a conventional operational health check for a service whose link operations depend on that store.

ambiguities.question: What qualifies as meaningful automated test coverage?
ambiguities.resolution: Tests must exercise every functional requirement and the important validation, authorization, expiry, rate-limit, persistence, and redirect failure paths; no numeric coverage percentage is required.
ambiguities.rationale: Behavior-focused coverage directly verifies the requested capabilities without inventing an arbitrary percentage threshold.

ambiguities.question: How many requests should the latency test use for warm-up, and should measured requests be concurrent?
ambiguities.resolution: Use 1,000 sequential warm-up requests followed by the 1,000 measured requests from a single client.
ambiguities.rationale: The human decision specifies a warm-up and a single client but not its size or concurrency; a fixed sequential warm-up makes the test repeatable and allows runtime initialization.

acceptance_criteria: Given a valid HTTP or HTTPS URL and no optional fields, when a client POSTs it to /api/links, then the service returns 201 with an 8-character code, a relative shortPath, and a management token shown only in that response.

Given a valid custom alias and future expiry, when a client creates the link, then the service returns 201 and the metadata contains the alias, original URL, creation timestamp, and normalized UTC expiry timestamp.

Given a custom alias shorter than 3 characters, longer than 32 characters, containing disallowed characters, or reserved for a service path, when a client creates a link, then the service returns 400.
Given an alias already assigned to an active link or tombstone, when a client creates a link with that alias, then the service returns 409 Conflict.

Given an invalid URL, a URL over 2,048 characters, a non-HTTP(S) scheme, localhost, or a host that is or resolves to a prohibited IPv4 or IPv6 address, when a client creates a link, then the service rejects it with HTTP 400 and does not create a link.

Given a hostname that fails DNS resolution or resolves to any prohibited address among its results, when a client creates a link, then the service rejects it; after a link is created, the service does not fetch its destination.
Given an active, unexpired link, when a client GETs /{code}, then the service returns 302 with the original URL in Location and Cache-Control: no-store.
Given an expired link, when a client GETs /{code}, then the service returns 410 and does not redirect; when a client GETs /api/links/{code}, then the service still returns its public metadata.
Given an unknown or deleted code, when a client GETs /{code} or GETs /api/links/{code}, then the service returns 404.
Given an active link, when a client GETs /api/links/{code} without credentials, then the service returns HTTP 200 with the original URL, created timestamp, and expiry value.
Given an active link, when a client DELETEs /api/links/{code} with its management token, then the service returns 204, erases the destination, and retains a tombstone reserving the code.
Given a missing or invalid management token for an active link deletion, when a client sends DELETE, then the service returns 401 or 403 respectively and does not delete the link.
Given a deleted code, when a client visits it, then the service returns 404; when a client attempts to create a link using that alias, then the service returns 409.

Given 20 create requests from one client IP within the configured minute, when that IP sends a further create request while limited, then the service returns 429 with Retry-After; a service restart resets the in-memory limit.
Given a created link or tombstone, when the service restarts using the same ./data store, then the link or reserved tombstone remains available and Flyway migrations have been applied.
Given the service and H2 store are available, when an operations client GETs /health, then it receives HTTP 200; when persistence is unavailable, then it receives HTTP 503.

Given the automated redirect latency test, when it performs 1,000 sequential warm-up requests followed by 1,000 measured requests from a single client on the local machine, then the measured in-process p99 is below 50 ms.
Given the automated test suite, when it runs, then it exercises every functional requirement and the specified important success and failure paths.
